prompt: A language requires some a characters followed by fewer b characters. Choose a witness with exactly one more a than b, and with the b-run as long as the arbitrary pumping length. Every legal non-empty pumped piece y contains only a characters. Which number of copies gives a contradiction?

options.explanation: Pumping up adds a’s while leaving the b count fixed. The new a count is p plus one plus k, so the strict inequality still holds.
Correct. Deleting the piece leaves p plus one minus k a’s, at most p because k is at least one. There are still p b’s, so the strict inequality fails.
One copy gives the original string s, which is in L by construction. It can never give a contradiction.

options.text: No i works; this language is regular
options.explanation: It is not regular: a DFA would need to compare unbounded counts. The proof just needs the right direction.

workedExample: The witness starts only one a ahead. Deleting any non-empty piece of a characters loses that lead, while leaving all b characters unchanged. The result has no more a characters than b characters, so it is outside the language. Repeating the piece instead increases the lead and cannot break this witness.

prompt: For the square-length language, choose a run whose length is the pumping length squared. Any legal pumped piece is non-empty and no longer than the pumping length. Why does adding one extra copy break membership?

options.text: It increases the length but cannot reach the next square
options.explanation: Correct. The gap to the next square is larger than the maximum allowed addition.

options.text: Every length increase destroys a square
options.explanation: A large enough increase could reach another square; the bound on the piece is essential.
Only the pumped piece is copied, not the whole witness.

options.text: The adversary must choose a piece of length one
options.explanation: The proof must handle every legal length, not one chosen split.

workedExample: The chosen length is already a square. The non-empty piece makes the new length strictly larger. Its length is bounded by the pumping length, while the gap to the next square is more than twice that length. The result lies between consecutive squares, so it cannot be a square.

prompt: In a prime-length pumping proof, the repetition count is chosen after the adversary reveals the piece length. Why is it useful to make the resulting length a product of two integers both at least two?

options.text: Any longer string has composite length
options.explanation: There are larger primes, so length increase alone proves nothing.

options.text: Every non-empty pumped piece has prime length
options.explanation: The split can give any permitted positive length.

options.text: The product guarantees a non-prime length for every legal split
options.explanation: Correct. Two factors greater than one certify compositeness, independently of the particular split.

options.text: A product proves the language is regular
options.explanation: The construction produces a contradiction to pumpability, not a finite automaton.

workedExample: Choose a prime witness sufficiently longer than the pumping length. After seeing the piece length, choose repetitions so the new total factors into two integers greater than one. This forces the result outside the prime-length language. The chosen repetition count may depend on the split; the proof still has to work for every legal split.
